gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of the charger's output the heater uses or how much energy one cold start costs: Redodo's 100 W pads take 34% of its own recommended 14.6 V 20 A charger's 292 W output (68% of a 10 A charger's 146 W), and Redodo's 165Ah model uses about 150 Wh (7.1% of its 2,112 Wh) to warm up from 14°F.
standout_why: I could not open the cited rival page (Power Queen: SSL certificate error) or most of the top results (SOK: 404; Battle Born, Renogy at reservepowerco, Rich Solar at offgridstores and the PowerUrus product page: HTTP 429; Vatrer product page: 403; ECO-Lithium PDF: SSL error), so the comparison rests on ChatGPT's answer and on the store listings I could read. ChatGPT's answer gives a heater wattage (Redodo 100 W) and Power Queen's 10 A minimum charge current to start heating. Neither says what share of the charge input the heater takes or how many Wh a warm-up uses. The Redodo and Vatrer store listings give trigger and stop temperatures and say heating runs on charging power, but they give no ratio either. I could not check whether the unread pages state such a ratio, so this is a 2, not a 3.
decides: This is a secondary point, not the main choice. With a small charger or a weak winter solar array, the heater takes a large share of the input before any charge reaches the cells. A shopper should size the charger to at least 2–3 times the heater wattage, and Redodo's own 20 A charger meets that for its 100 W heater. On cost per Wh, the pick holds: the Redodo 12V 100Ah at $251.99 ($0.197/Wh) costs less per Wh than the Vatrer heated Group 24 at $299.99 ($0.234/Wh, pre-order). Shoppers who need more capacity in one battery get the lowest cost per Wh here from the Vatrer 12V 300Ah self-heating ($0.164/Wh).

This assumes the pads run from charger input, which the copy implies ('charging halts until the heating pads raise the temperature') but does not say outright.
